learningObjectives.text: Explain how geologists investigate Earth's interior using indirect evidence.
Compare the crust, mantle, and core by composition and position.
Distinguish Earth's physical layers by their mechanical behavior.
Explain how density, pressure, and temperature change with depth inside Earth.
Compare P and S waves and explain how their speeds and paths change inside Earth.
Use seismic-wave shadow zones to infer the structure and liquid outer core of Earth.
Explain how gravity measurements relate to Earth's geoid and internal mass distribution.
Explain isostasy and how crustal density affects elevation.
Explain how internal heat drives mantle convection.
Describe how motion in Earth's outer core generates its magnetic field.
Explain how seismic reflection imaging reveals subsurface structure.
Summarize Wegener's continental-drift hypothesis and the evidence supporting it.
Explain how evidence developed in the 1950s and 1960s established plate tectonics.
Distinguish Earth's crust, mantle, core, and lithosphere.
Classify plate margins as convergent, divergent, or transform.
Explain how subduction occurs at convergent boundaries and identify its results.
Compare continental collision with subduction and relate collision to supercontinent assembly.
Explain how divergent boundaries form rifts and triple junctions.
Use magnetic stripes to explain seafloor spreading and determine spreading rates.
Describe transform-boundary motion and the features it produces.
Explain the forces that move plates and summarize the Wilson Cycle.
Explain how hotspots and mantle plumes produce volcanic activity away from plate boundaries.
Define a mineral using the five required criteria.
Distinguish minerals from glass, synthetic materials, and amber using the mineral criteria.
Explain how atoms, chemical bonds, isotopes, and polymorphs relate to mineral properties.
Describe crystal growth and distinguish the six crystal systems.
Explain the main processes by which minerals form.
Identify minerals using color, streak, and luster.
Use the Mohs scale to compare mineral hardness.
Distinguish cleavage from fracture using mineral breakage patterns.
Use special physical properties to identify minerals.
Identify the major elements in Earth and its crust.
Describe the silica tetrahedron and compare the main silicate structures.
Recognize common rock-forming minerals and distinguish silicates from nonsilicates.
Distinguish magma from lava and intrusive rocks from extrusive rocks.
Explain decompression, volatile addition, and heat transfer as ways rocks melt.
Relate melting processes to their tectonic settings.
Compare magmas by silica content, density, and viscosity.
Explain how source composition, melting, and crystallization produce different melts.
Explain fractional crystallization and use Bowen's reaction series to predict mineral order.
Classify igneous rocks by texture and composition using the classification chart.
Identify igneous textures and distinguish fragmental rocks.
Distinguish dikes from sills by their relationship to surrounding rock layers.
Identify plutons and batholiths and explain how they become exposed.
Compare the main volcano types by shape and eruption products.
Explain how water drives weathering and transports sediment.
Compare physical and chemical weathering and explain how surface area affects weathering rate.
Identify mechanical weathering processes and explain how they break rock apart.
Explain chemical weathering and how it produces differential weathering.
Explain how climate and parent material affect soil formation and soil horizons.
Classify soils using their horizons and the criteria covered in the lesson.
Define sediment and distinguish clastic, biochemical, organic, and chemical sedimentary rocks.
Explain how clastic sedimentary rocks form and classify them by grain size, sorting, and composition.
Distinguish biochemical, organic, and chemical sedimentary rocks by how they form.
Identify bedding, formations, and common sedimentary structures in rock exposures.
Relate depositional environments to the sedimentary features of deltas.
Explain how basins, sea-level change, and facies relate to sediment deposition.
Define metamorphism and identify a protolith as the rock before metamorphism.
Explain how metamorphism changes rock texture and produces foliation.
Describe the five processes that change rocks during metamorphism.
Explain how heat, pressure, differential stress, and fluids alter rocks.
Identify foliated rocks and place them along the metamorphic-grade sequence.
Recognize common nonfoliated metamorphic rocks and their protoliths.
Relate metamorphic grade, index minerals, and facies to pressure and temperature conditions.
Compare contact metamorphism with other types of metamorphism.
Distinguish dynamic from regional metamorphism by setting and process.
Compare hydrothermal, subduction, burial, and shock metamorphism.
Explain how metamorphic rocks return to the surface and relate shields to exposed ancient crust.
Explain deep time and why geologic time dwarfs human history.
State uniformitarianism (?the present is the key to the past?), identify Hutton?s contribution, and describe Lyell?s role.
Distinguish relative age (older or younger) from numerical age (years).
Apply original horizontality, superposition, lateral continuity, cross-cutting relations, baked contacts, and inclusions.
Recognize and sketch angular unconformities, nonconformities, and disconformities.
Read a block diagram and place its geologic events in order.
Use fossil succession, index fossils, and fossil ranges (FAD/LAD) for relative dating.
Explain formations, stratigraphic columns, correlation, and geologic maps.
Describe how the composite geologic column became the geologic time scale of eons, eras, periods, and epochs.
Explain radioactive decay, parent and daughter isotopes, and half-life; solve half-life calculations.
Explain what an isotopic date records (closure temperature) and identify which rocks can be dated.
Describe non-radiometric numerical dating using tree rings, growth bands, varves, and ice layers.
Bracket the age of sedimentary layers using datable igneous rocks.
State Earth?s age and describe the evidence used to determine it.
Explain the principle of fossil succession and use fossil ranges to date and match rock layers.
Define FAD and LAD, and explain why overlapping ranges narrow down an age.
Explain what makes a good index fossil.
Place major events in the history of life on the geologic time scale.
Name and describe the eight types of fossilization, with an example of each.
Describe the steps that turn a dead animal into a fossil exposed at the surface.
Explain why fossilization is rare and why the fossil record is biased.
Explain how scientists infer what extinct organisms did using observation, analogy, and analysis.
Describe stromatolites and explain how cyanobacteria changed Earth?s atmosphere.
Recognize common invertebrate fossils, including trilobites, brachiopods, and ammonites.
Explain why the Burgess Shale is special and why new fossil sites matter.
Explain natural selection and how new species form.
Compare background and mass extinction, and interpret the five major drops on the extinction graph.
Explain how DNA provides a partial record of evolutionary history, including the carpenter bee example.
Describe the Hadean Eon and the early molten Earth.
Explain how arcs and greenstone belts contributed to the growth of the first continents.
Summarize evidence for Archean rocks and early life.
Explain how cratons formed and how they contributed to the assembly of North America.
Describe Proterozoic oxygenation and the growth of large continents.
Describe evidence for major glaciations on the early Earth.
Relate Paleozoic seas, orogens, terranes, and Pangaea to changing geography.
Summarize major Paleozoic biological events, including the end-Permian extinction.
Explain how Pangaea broke apart and how western North America developed during the Mesozoic.
Describe major Mesozoic events and evidence for the age of dinosaurs.
Explain the evidence for the K?Pg impact and its consequences for life.
Relate Cenozoic continental movement to the Basin and Range, mountain building, and ice ages.
Summarize the rise and diversification of mammals during the Cenozoic.
Define deformation, stress, and strain and explain how they are related.
Compare compression, tension, and shear by the changes they cause in rock.
Distinguish brittle from ductile rock behavior and identify conditions that favor each.
Distinguish joints from veins and explain how each forms.
Identify faults as fractures along which rock has moved.
Use offset layers and other fault clues to determine the direction of movement.
Explain how rock layers bend to form folds.
Identify anticlines, synclines, and plunging folds from their geometry.
Distinguish domes, basins, and cleavage by their structure.
Explain how collision builds crustal roots and relates to isostasy.
Compare the effects of subduction and rifting on Earth's crust.
Explain how cratons, delamination, and basins relate to crustal evolution.
Define mass movement and identify which downslope processes qualify.
Explain how gravity, slope, water, and material strength contribute to slope failure.
Distinguish slow creep from slumping by movement and landform evidence.
Compare mudflows, debris flows, and lahars by their material and triggers.
Distinguish landslides from falls by how material moves downslope.
Explain how water and weak layers can destabilize a slope.
Explain how submarine landslides occur and describe their potential consequences.
Explain how elastic strain builds and is released during fault rupture.
Use fault geometry and block motion to identify the relative movement of rocks.
Distinguish an earthquake's focus from its epicenter and explain how seismographs record shaking.
Compare body waves with surface waves by their paths, motion, and effects.
Distinguish magnitude from intensity and relate earthquake magnitude to energy release.
Explain how ground conditions affect shaking and earthquake damage.
Explain how tsunamis form and compare the roles of warnings and prediction.

scale.title: Scale of the Universe & Patterns in the Sky
scale.subject: astr207

learningObjectives.text: Place Earth within the Solar System, the Milky Way, and the observable universe.
Compare astronomical distance units and choose an appropriate unit for a given scale.
Explain how the finite speed of light lets astronomers observe objects as they were in the past.
Use a scale model to compare distances and sizes across the universe.
Summarize the Big Bang, stellar life cycles, and how stars produce elements.
Use the cosmic calendar to relate the history of the universe to a one-year timescale.
Describe Earth's rotation, orbit, and motion through the Milky Way.
Explain how observations support cosmic expansion and describe the raisin-bread analogy and dark energy.
Explain how constellations map onto the celestial sphere.
Use angular size to describe objects in the local sky.
Predict which objects rise and set using the observer's latitude.
Compare a sidereal day with a solar day and explain why their lengths differ.
Compare a sidereal month with a synodic month and explain why their lengths differ.
Compare a sidereal year with a tropical year and explain why their lengths differ.
Use orbital periods to predict conjunctions and identify when transits can occur.
Use the Sun's apparent motion to explain local solar time.
Convert between standard time zones and Universal Time.
Explain how daylight saving time changes civil clock time.
Explain how leap years keep calendars aligned with Earth's orbit.
Describe the Sun's apparent daily and annual motion across the sky.
Explain how the Sun's path changes at the equator and in the tropics.
Explain the Sun's path and daylight patterns at the poles and polar circles.
Use noon-Sun altitude and sky coordinates to determine an object's position.
Use sky coordinates and observed Sun or star positions to determine location.
State Newton's three laws and explain how they describe motion.
Distinguish speed from velocity and calculate each from motion data.
Explain how changes in speed or direction produce acceleration.
Describe the direction and value of acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface.
Relate mass to inertia and momentum.
Determine net force from the forces acting on an object.
Distinguish mass from weight and calculate weight from mass and gravitational acceleration.
Explain why orbiting astronauts experience apparent weightlessness.
Apply Newton's first law to predict motion when the net force is zero.
Apply Newton's second law to relate net force, mass, and acceleration.
Use Newton's third law to identify action?reaction force pairs.
Define energy and distinguish kinetic, potential, and thermal energy.
Identify the main forms of energy and describe how they differ.
Calculate kinetic energy from an object's mass and speed.
Distinguish thermal energy from temperature and explain how they are related.
Explain how gravitational potential energy depends on position in a gravitational field.
Explain how mass and energy are related by E = mc?.
Apply conservation of energy to track energy transfers and transformations.
Apply conservation of momentum to predict the outcome of an interaction.
Use momentum conservation to analyze one-dimensional collisions.
Explain how torque changes angular momentum.
Use conservation of angular momentum to explain why rotation speeds up as radius decreases.
Distinguish conservation of energy, momentum, and angular momentum and identify when each applies.
Explain how gravitational force depends on the masses and separation of two objects.
Use the inverse-square relationship to predict how gravitational force changes with distance.
Distinguish bound elliptical orbits from parabolic and hyperbolic trajectories.
Use Newton's version of Kepler's third law to infer the masses of orbiting systems.
Explain how orbital energy is conserved along an orbit.
Explain how an orbit gains or loses energy through interactions.
Define escape velocity and explain how it depends on gravitational binding.
Explain how differences in gravitational pull across an object produce tides.
Explain how tidal friction affects the Earth?Moon system and leads to synchronous rotation.
Explain why objects in the same gravitational field fall at the same acceleration when air resistance is negligible.
Describe how light carries energy from a source to an observer.
Explain how a prism separates white light into component colors.
Compare the main ways light interacts with matter.
Describe light as an electromagnetic wave and identify its key properties.
Relate amplitude, wavelength, frequency, and speed for a wave.
Use c = ?f to relate the wavelength and frequency of light.
Relate a light wave's wavelength to its color.
Describe light as photons and relate photon energy to frequency.
Explain how light can transfer energy to charged particles.
Order the electromagnetic spectrum by wavelength and frequency.
Identify the parts of an atom and describe their charges and locations.
Use atomic number and mass number to distinguish isotopes and ions.
Compare the phases of matter and explain how pressure affects them.
Explain how heating and cooling cause phase changes.
Explain how changes in atomic energy levels produce photon emission or absorption.
Explain how relative motion changes the observed wavelength through the Doppler effect.
Distinguish redshift from blueshift and relate each to line-of-sight motion.
Explain why the Doppler effect measures only motion toward or away from an observer.
Use Doppler shifts to interpret the rotation of galaxies and stars.
Calculate line-of-sight speed from a measured Doppler shift.
Distinguish continuous, emission, and absorption spectra.
Explain how thermal spectra reveal an object's temperature.
Compare how the eye and a camera form images.
Explain how telescope aperture affects light collection and how telescope design affects image sharpness.
Identify the properties of astronomical objects that can be measured from their light.
Explain how Earth's atmosphere affects observations and compare observing sites.
Compare what astronomers can learn from spectra and from non-visible astronomical messengers.
Interpret a map of the Solar System and identify major orbital patterns.
Compare terrestrial and jovian worlds by their defining properties.
Compare Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars by their atmospheres, surface conditions, and evidence of past activity.
Compare Jupiter and Saturn as gas giants with Uranus and Neptune as ice giants.
Distinguish asteroids, comets, and dwarf planets.
Use patterns among Solar System objects to infer clues about the system's history.
Describe how spacecraft investigate other worlds and compare mission types.
Recall how Homo sapiens is classified, and compare eukaryotic cells with prokaryotic cells.
Compare how molecules cross the plasma membrane, and describe the cell parts that make and package proteins.
Describe the tissue types and the germ layers they come from, and locate body structures using anatomical planes.
Describe the phases of the cell cycle and the roles of interphase, mitosis, and cytokinesis.
Compare mitosis and meiosis, including their products, chromosome numbers, and genetic variation.
Explain how mutations and chromosome-number errors occur, and how checkpoints relate to cancer.
Trace gene expression from DNA to protein and explain how regulation produces different cell types.
Sequence fertilization, cleavage, implantation, and gastrulation in early development.
Describe the organization and functions of the central and peripheral nervous systems.
Explain how action potentials and neurotransmitters transmit nervous-system signals.
Compare major neuron and glial-cell types by structure and function.
Describe the developmental origins of the central and peripheral nervous systems.
Compare skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle by structure, control, and function.
Trace skeletal muscle organization from the whole muscle to the sarcomere.
Explain how a motor-neuron signal triggers skeletal-muscle contraction.
Describe how cardiac and smooth muscle contract and perform their roles.
Explain the embryonic origins of muscle tissue and tendons.
Describe bone tissue and identify the structures of a long bone.
Explain bone remodeling and the stages of fracture repair.
Identify the major bones and regions of the axial and appendicular skeleton.
Compare joint structures and relate joint type to movement.
Compare bone formation and growth, including the embryonic origins of the skeleton.
Describe the parts and functions of the gastrointestinal tract and accessory organs, and trace how food moves through the tract.
Compare how nutrients are digested and absorbed, explain the gut microbiome?s roles, and describe the embryonic origin of the GI system.
Describe the upper and lower airway and the function of each part.
Explain how muscles drive breathing, how gases are exchanged in the lungs and tissues, and how gases are carried in blood.
Explain how breathing is regulated and monitored, and describe the embryonic origin of the respiratory system.
Describe the components and functions of blood, and explain blood groups and transfusion compatibility.
Compare the structure and roles of arteries, arterioles, capillaries, and veins.
Identify the heart?s chambers, valves, layers, and electrical conduction pathway.
Trace blood through the pulmonary and systemic circuits and relate major vessels to the heart.
Explain the cardiac cycle and how the heart and vessels regulate blood pressure.
Describe how the cardiovascular system develops, including the transition at the first breath.
